name: Kabi Lungchok

local_name.name: Kabi Lungchok (also spelled Kabi Longstok)
local_name.meaning: Commonly translated as 'stone erected by our blood', the stones that mark the blood-brotherhood oath

tagline: The stones where Sikkim's blood-brotherhood oath is remembered
meta_description: Kabi Lungchok, about 17 km from Gangtok: the memorial stones of the Lepcha and Bhutia blood-brotherhood treaty. No permit for Indians, costs, timings and tips.
summary: Kabi Lungchok is a memorial site about 17 km north of Gangtok on the North Sikkim Highway, where Sikkimese tradition places the blood-brotherhood oath between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia prince Khye Bumsa, in the 13th century. Stone pillars mark the place. It lies below the protected areas, so Indian visitors need no permit.
intro: Kabi Lungchok is a quiet forest clearing beside the North Sikkim Highway, roughly 17 km and 45 minutes to an hour from Gangtok. Stone pillars stand here to mark the place where, in Sikkim's own histories, a Bhutia prince named Khye Bumsa and a Lepcha chief named Thekong Tek swore a treaty of blood brotherhood. Wikipedia's article on the site gives the literal meaning of the name as 'stone erected by our blood'.

The oath matters because of what it stands for. Sikkim's migration narratives describe the Lepcha as the earlier people of the land and the Bhutia as newcomers from Tibet, and the treaty is remembered as the moment the two agreed to live together. The oath is dated by tradition to the 13th century and is not recorded in a contemporary document, so it is best read as Sikkim's founding story rather than a dated fact.

For travellers it is a short, free stop of 20 to 40 minutes that fits easily into a day on the North Sikkim road. Walk the grove slowly, read the plaque and leave the stones alone. Kabi Lungchok is in Mangan district but outside the protected areas, so no protected area permit is needed for Indian visitors. Check current status before you travel.

story.title: The oath of two peoples
story.text: Wikipedia's article on Kabi Lungchok tells the story as Sikkim's histories tell it. Khye Bumsa, a prince from the Minyak house in eastern Tibet, settled in the Chumbi valley and sought the blessing of the Lepcha religious leader Thekong Tek, whose blessing is said to have brought him sons. Thekong Tek had no children of his own, and a prophecy held that Khye Bumsa's descendants would rule. The two men then swore a treaty of blood brotherhood at Kabi Lungchok. The oath recorded in the article is that Khye Bumsa would not discriminate against his new Lepcha subjects. Stone pillars were later raised to mark the place, and Wikipedia notes that ritual prayers are held each year to commemorate the treaty. Khye Bumsa's grandson Phuntsog Namgyal was crowned the first Chogyal at Yuksom in 1642. The event itself belongs to oral tradition and later Sikkimese histories, and its details differ between tellings, so we give it as tradition and not as a dated record.
story.source: Wikipedia, Kabi Lungchok and Khye Bumsa (Sikkimese migration narratives)

little_known.fact: The name is pronounced roughly 'Kayu sha bhi Lungchok' and is translated as 'stone erected by our blood'. Wikipedia also records the spelling Kabi Longstok.

The forest around the site is subtropical mixed broad-leaved hill forest, with trees such as Nepal alder, Castanopsis and Toona ciliata listed, and several waterfalls nearby, one known as the Seven Sisters.
Thekong Tek, the Lepcha signatory, is described in Sikkim's histories as a religious leader, and the treaty is the first bond between the Lepcha and the Bhutia in the Sikkimese narrative.

facts: Lepcha and Bhutia blood-brotherhood treaty site
Not needed for Indian visitors; foreigners need the Sikkim restricted area permit

highlights.title: The memorial stones
highlights.text: A circle of upright stones marks the spot of the treaty, with a plaque that tells the story in brief. The site is small and the atmosphere quiet. Walk around the stones rather than over them, keep voices low and do not climb or sit on the pillars.

highlights.title: Statues of the two leaders
highlights.text: Statues of Khye Bumsa and Thekong Tek stand at the site, representing the two peoples who swore the oath. They make a good starting point for explaining the story to children. Please do not touch or lean on them.

highlights.title: A forest setting
highlights.text: The site sits in subtropical broad-leaved forest beside the highway, with streams and waterfalls close by. Birdsong is easy to hear in the early morning, and the air is a few degrees warmer than in Gangtok.

highlights.title: A natural pause on the road north
highlights.text: Kabi Lungchok breaks the drive between Gangtok and Phodong, Mangan or Lachung. A 20 to 40 minute stop costs nothing, and it pairs well with Tashi View Point before it and the Seven Sisters Waterfall after it.

highlights.title: A story that still matters
highlights.text: The oath is remembered each year in prayers at the site, and in the festival of Pang Lhabsol, which Sikkimese accounts also connect with the bond between Lepcha and Bhutia. For many Sikkimese, this is a place of respect rather than a photo stop.

how_to_reach.text: There is no shared jeep to Kabi Lungchok as such. Shared jeeps to Mangan from Gangtok pass the site, and the driver may stop if you ask in advance, though this is not guaranteed. Fares to Mangan are roughly ₹300 to 450 a seat, indicative.

A reserved small car from Gangtok takes about 45 minutes to an hour for roughly 17 km. A half-day car covering Tashi View Point and Kabi Lungchok is indicatively ₹1,800 to 2,500. NH10 and the North Sikkim Highway can close after monsoon slides.
Go to Gangtok first, which takes 4.5 to 5 hours from either on NH10, longer via Kalimpong or Algarah when NH10 is closed by slides. Visit Kabi Lungchok on a morning from Gangtok or on your way north.

costs: Shared jeep Gangtok to Mangan (passes the site)
Half-day reserved small car with Tashi View Point
Free, as far as we know
where_to_stay: There are no tourist stays at Kabi Lungchok itself and we do not plan nights here. Most visitors stay in Gangtok and visit on a morning or on the way north. For a night closer to Phodong and Labrang, ask us about small homestays and lodges in the Phodong area, and for the next planned halt on the North Sikkim road, Mangan has simple hotels. Budget rooms in Gangtok run about ₹1,500 to 3,000, and better hotels there cost more.
tips: Go in the morning, when the light is soft and the site is quiet.
Keep your voice low and do not climb on or sit on the stones.
Carry a refillable bottle and a rain jacket, because the forest is damp for much of the year.
Pair the stop with Tashi View Point before it and the Seven Sisters Waterfall and Phodong after it.
Ask your driver about road status before leaving Gangtok in the monsoon, when slides are common.

experiences.title: Standing at the blood-brotherhood stones
experiences.summary: Spend half an hour among the stone pillars and statues at Kabi Lungchok, where Sikkim's histories place the oath between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia prince Khye Bumsa. A short stop that explains how Sikkim's peoples tell their own beginning.
body: The site is small: a clearing in the forest, a plaque and a ring of upright stones, with statues of the two leaders. Read the plaque first, then walk the edge of the ring. In Wikipedia's account, the oath was that Khye Bumsa would not discriminate against his Lepcha subjects, and the stones were raised to mark it.

Take a few minutes to think about what the site is for. It is not a battlefield or a palace, and nothing was built here. It is a place where two peoples are remembered as having made a promise, which is one reason it matters to many Sikkimese families.

Keep your visit simple. Do not climb on the stones, do not touch the statues and ask before photographing anyone who has come to pray. If you are with children, tell the story in two sentences before you arrive and let them look. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: As far as we know, no. It is an open memorial site beside the highway, and we have not seen a ticket counter. Arrangements can change, so ask your driver or check current status before you travel. If you plan to visit on a festival or prayer day, expect more visitors.

faqs.q: How long should we spend at Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: Twenty to forty minutes is enough to read the plaque, walk around the stones and take a few photographs. If you want to sit quietly or look for birds in the forest around it, allow an hour. Most tour cars stop for about twenty minutes.

faqs.q: Is Kabi Lungchok suitable for children and older people?
faqs.a: Yes. The site is close to the road and mostly level, though paths can be damp and slippery after rain. Wear shoes with grip. There is little shade or shelter, so carry a rain jacket in the monsoon and a hat in summer. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Telling the oath story to children
experiences.image_query: Lepcha Bhutia treaty Kabi Lungchok statues
experiences.summary: A simple way to bring Sikkim's founding story to life for children: read a short summary in the car, stand at the stones, and talk about why the two peoples promised each other. We give a plain version with its source.
body: The story is easy to tell in a minute. In Sikkim's histories, Khye Bumsa, a prince from Tibet, and Thekong Tek, a Lepcha religious leader, became friends. They swore an oath of blood brotherhood at this place so that Lepcha and Bhutia would live together as one people. Wikipedia's articles on Kabi Lungchok and Khye Bumsa give the story and its sources.

Make it a game on the drive from Gangtok. Ask children to guess what the stones are for, then give the answer at the site. Point to the statues of the two leaders, and ask what a promise means to them. Talk about the different peoples of Sikkim, Lepcha, Bhutia, Limbu, Nepali and others, and how they share one state.

Tell children plainly that this is a story passed down through tradition, and that historians differ on its details. That honesty is better than presenting it as proven history, and it makes a good first lesson in how places remember their past. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the story of Kabi Lungchok in simple words?
faqs.a: In Sikkim's histories, the Bhutia prince Khye Bumsa and the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek swore an oath of blood brotherhood here so that their two peoples would live as friends. The stones mark the spot. The story is tradition, set in the 13th century, and not a dated written record.

faqs.q: Is the Kabi Lungchok story true?
faqs.a: It is a founding tradition, told in Sikkimese histories and retold on Wikipedia. The treaty is dated to the 13th century by tradition, with no contemporary document, and details differ between tellings. That does not make the site less meaningful: the stones and prayers are real, and the oath is honoured today.

faqs.q: What age is right for this stop?
faqs.a: Any age can enjoy it, though children under about eight may need the story kept short. Older children and teenagers usually engage with the idea of an oath between two peoples. Children under 5 cannot enter North Sikkim protected areas, but Kabi Lungchok is outside them. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Early bird walk around Kabi forest
experiences.best_time: Early morning, March to May and October to November
experiences.summary: A slow early walk along the highway edge and forest tracks near Kabi Lungchok. The surrounding subtropical hill forest is recorded as home to many bird species, so patient visitors with binoculars can expect good birdsong and, with luck, some sightings.
body: Wikipedia's article on Kabi Lungchok, citing the ENVIS Centre for Sikkim, lists birds recorded in the area, including the crested serpent eagle, rufous-necked hornbill, Ward's trogon and black-breasted parrotbill. We do not promise any of them. Several are shy or rare, but the forest is real, and a patient morning walk can turn up common hill birds and an occasional surprise.

Start at first light, when the highway is quiet. Walk along the verges and listen before looking: much of the forest is heard rather than seen. Binoculars help. A local guide knows the calls, and your driver may know the best stretches. Stay on tracks and away from the road's outer edge, where traffic and slides are risks.

Mid-March to May and October to November are the more pleasant months. In the monsoon the roads are risky and leeches are common. Carry water, a rain jacket and shoes with grip. Check current status before you travel, and do not play recorded calls to attract birds.

faqs.q: Which birds can I see near Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: Wikipedia's article, citing ENVIS Sikkim, lists the pariah kite, crested serpent eagle, rufous-necked hornbill, chestnut-breasted partridge, black-breasted parrotbill, grey-crowned prinia and Ward's trogon. Sightings are never guaranteed and some are rare. Expect common hill birds on an ordinary morning. A guide improves your odds.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to bird-watch here?
faqs.a: No protected area permit is needed for Indian visitors at Kabi Lungchok, which is below the protected areas. Foreign nationals need their Sikkim restricted area permit, applied online since January 2026. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk along the highway?
faqs.a: Walk only where there is a verge, keep to the inner side and listen for vehicles, as the North Sikkim Highway is a working road with blind bends. Avoid the walk in heavy rain, when slides are common. Do not step into the forest off the track alone, and tell your driver where you are going.

experiences.title: Gangtok to Phodong day loop by car
experiences.best_time: October to May, leaving by 8:30 am
experiences.image_query: North Sikkim Highway Phodong Kabi road
experiences.summary: Hire a small car for a day loop up the North Sikkim Highway: Tashi View Point, Kabi Lungchok, the Seven Sisters Waterfall, Phodong Monastery and Labrang Monastery, then back to Gangtok. A rooted, permit-free day that costs less than most day tours.
body: Leave Gangtok by 8:30 am. First stop is Tashi View Point for the morning view, if the sky is clear. Next come Kabi Lungchok at about 17 km, the Seven Sisters Waterfall a little further on, and then Phodong Monastery at about 38 km and Labrang Monastery 2 km above it. Distances on this road are short, but the road is winding and slow.

A reserved small car for this loop runs about ₹3,000 to 4,500, indicative, depending on the driver, the season and how long you stay. Entry to the sites is free as far as we know, though monasteries may ask for a small donation. Take food or have lunch at Phodong, which has simple eating places.

No protected area permit is needed for Indian travellers on this stretch. The loop is easy to add at the start or end of a North Sikkim trip. In the monsoon, slides can close the road, so check current status before you travel and allow a margin on the return.

faqs.q: How long does the Gangtok to Phodong loop take?
faqs.a: Allow 6 to 8 hours including stops: about 1.5 hours each way to Phodong at 38 km, plus 30 to 40 minutes each at Kabi Lungchok and the monasteries and a short stop at the waterfall. Leave by 8:30 am to be back before dusk, and longer if the road is slow.

faqs.q: Is the loop possible in the monsoon?
faqs.a: It is possible on dry days, but slides and waterlogged stretches are common from June to September, and the road may close at short notice. We would plan the loop for October to May if you can. In the monsoon, check current status before you travel and keep your schedule flexible.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for the loop?
faqs.a: No protected area permit is needed for Indian travellers on Gangtok, Kabi Lungchok, Seven Sisters Waterfall, Phodong and Labrang. Foreign nationals need the online Sikkim restricted area permit to be in the state. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where is Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: Kabi Lungchok is about 17 km north of Gangtok on the North Sikkim Highway, in Mangan district (North Sikkim). It stands in forest beside the road, a little before the Seven Sisters Waterfall and Phodong. It takes roughly 45 minutes to an hour by car from Gangtok.

faqs.q: What happened at Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: According to Sikkim's histories, the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia prince Khye Bumsa swore an oath of blood brotherhood here in the 13th century, pledging friendship between their peoples. Stone pillars mark the site. It is a founding tradition rather than a dated written record.

faqs.q: What does Kabi Lungchok mean?
faqs.a: Wikipedia gives the literal meaning as 'stone erected by our blood', with the name pronounced roughly 'Kayu sha bhi Lungchok'. It is also spelled Kabi Longstok. The stones mark the place of the treaty between the Lepcha and the Bhutia, and are the reason the site is remembered.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: No protected area permit is needed for Indian visitors, as the site is outside the protected areas of Mangan district. Foreign nationals need the online Sikkim restricted area permit to be in the state. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much time do we need at Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: Twenty to forty minutes is enough for most visitors, who walk around the stones, read the plaque and take a few photographs. Add time if you want to watch birds in the forest around the site, or to combine it with the Seven Sisters Waterfall and Phodong.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee?
faqs.a: As far as we know, entry is free. It is an open memorial beside the highway. Fees and opening arrangements can change, and there may be a donation box or prayer events, so check current status before you travel and ask your driver or hotel in Gangtok.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: October to May is best, with the clearest weather in October, November, March and April. The monsoon from June to September brings heavy rain and slides on the highway, and the damp forest has leeches. A morning visit is quiet. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can we visit Kabi Lungchok on the way to Lachung or Mangan?
faqs.a: Yes. It is on the road north and makes a natural 20 to 40 minute stop, so ask your driver to include it. On a shared 2N/3D tour the schedule is fixed by the operator, and a stop may not be possible, so ask when booking. Tourist vehicles must cross the Toong check post by 4:00 pm.

faqs.q: Is Kabi Lungchok worth the stop?
faqs.a: Yes, if you care about how Sikkim's peoples tell their own story. It is a small, quiet site with no ticket and little to see beyond the stones, statues and plaque, so it suits a short stop and not a half-day trip. Combine it with the Seven Sisters Waterfall and Phodong.
